title: How CBT reshaped our understanding of psychology
description: This article explores the historical roots of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), starting from the 1960s and the work of psychologist Aaron Beck. We’ll highlight the key aspects of CBT in the context of an era dominated by psychoanalysis and present the arguments for why this approach is so effective.

texts: Let’s take a gentle look back at the past to understand who stood at the origins of cognitive behavioral therapy and how Sigmund Freud—a name indispensable to the history of psychology—fits into the story.
We won’t get bogged down in detailed dates and facts.
If this overview leaves you wanting more detail, you can always look it up on Wikipedia or in specialized sources.
Aaron Beck, a future star of psychology, was born in 1921.
As a child, he was shy, often fell ill, and was very afraid of doctors (ironic, wouldn’t you agree?).
However, instead of retreating from his fears, he decided to face them head-on: he attended Yale Medical School and later chose psychiatry.
“Fight fire with fire,” young Aaron might have thought as he overcame his fear of blood and spent hours in the operating room.
Initially, like many psychiatrists of that time, Beck practiced psychoanalysis.

But he soon realized that searching endlessly for roots in childhood experiences was like looking for your keys under a streetlight—not because you lost them there, but because that’s where the light is.
Beck was drawn to precision, verifiability, and data, rather than abstract constructs.
A figure as respected and famous as Freud needs no introduction, but let’s recap the basic principles of psychoanalysis:
The primary focus is on unconscious processes and childhood experiences.
Psychoanalysts explore past traumas, conflicts, and relationship dynamics to understand their influence on current difficulties.
<q author="Robert Orben">Psychoanalysis is when you pay $35 an hour to complain about yourself.</q>
Free-form conversation: the client shares their thoughts and feelings, while the therapist helps interpret potential unconscious motives.
The process can be long — sometimes lasting for years.
It is assumed that a significant part of our actions is driven by unconscious processes, often linked to suppressed desires and conflicts.
“It is a great mistake to believe that the roots of psychological problems must be sought in childhood experiences,” Beck wrote.
“It is far more important to understand what is happening in a person’s life right now, how they perceive themselves and the world around them, and how they think.”
Followers of Freud believed that depression was the result of anger directed inward.
But in the 1960s, while working with people experiencing depression, Beck noticed recurring negative thoughts — “I’m a failure,” “nobody loves me,” “the world is a terrible place.”

<q author="Stephen Hollem">Aaron Beck took a century-old dogma, found that it didn’t hold up to criticism, and created something simple, reliable, and effective, putting it in its place. He essentially saved psychotherapy from itself.</q>
These thoughts, like a broken record, significantly diminished their quality of life.
He asked himself: what if these thoughts aren’t just a side effect, but one of the key causes of suffering?
Instead of limiting the discussion to childhood experiences, Beck suggested trying to change current thinking patterns.
Beck conducted a series of studies that supported his hypothesis.
He developed questionnaires and methods to identify negative automatic thoughts, and then created cognitive therapy to teach people how to recognize and challenge these beliefs.
Later, he added behavioral methods to these cognitive techniques — and thus, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) was born.
Beck suggested focusing on current beliefs and interpretations of everyday events, rather than just on childhood conflicts.
He used practical exercises to help people notice and change unhelpful thoughts.
For example, he recommended keeping a journal to record negative thoughts and analyze them.
This helped people see how often their perception of reality was distorted and how that affected their mental well-being.
Unlike long-term psychoanalysis, which could last for years, Beck’s therapy usually took up to 12 months and proved highly effective.
I immediately felt anxious about my financial well-being.
After ten sessions, clients would tell me, “Doctor, thank you!
I’ve started looking at life differently and thinking about myself and others in a new way."
“I don’t need your help anymore!” — they’d say, thank you, and leave, while my income continued to drop.
However, his anxiety soon turned into confidence: the results spoke for themselves.

It suggests challenging negative beliefs and replacing them with more adaptive ones
It focuses primarily on childhood trauma

texts: Cognitive therapy helped people overcome depression faster and find practical solutions, making Beck so successful that he no longer had to worry about his finances.
The method spread rapidly, and by the early 1990s, seeing a cognitive psychologist had become as common as practicing yoga.
Of course, psychoanalysis and other approaches didn’t disappear.
Every person is unique, and no single method works for everyone.
Today, many specialists use an integrative approach, combining elements of psychoanalysis with other techniques.
At the same time, CBT remains one of the most researched and evidence-based approaches.
It is used all over the world, and Beck’s name has become iconic among specialists.
His ideas continue to inspire a new generation of therapists helping people navigate internal conflicts and find more helpful ways of interacting with the world.
Now that you know a little more about the history, we invite those interested to dive deeper on their own.
And the rest of you — to continue the journey with us.
We truly value CBT (and we don’t just say that).
In our work, we rely on a scientific approach: all techniques are based on proven data.
That’s why the next section is dedicated to evidence of the method’s efficacy.
Get ready for some numbers!
We warned you!
